568.title: The month of Jeth
568.hook: in Jeth, join with the One before whom all bow (Barah Maha, ang 134)
568.howItsDone: On the sangrand of Jeth, gurdwaras that keep the day read the Jeth stanza of Guru Arjan's Barah Maha, and in the summer heat, especially around the remembrance of Guru Arjan's martyrdom, Sikhs set up chhabeel stalls serving cold sweetened water to passersby.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Vaisakh, and your line: vaisakh: longing. Did you make the call? The harvest is in. Now the heat arrives, and the third month asks for something new. Day five hundred sixty-eight.

By late morning the roads shimmer. Shops pull their shutters halfway down. This is Jeth, roughly May into June in Punjab, hot in a way that changes how people live. Anyone who can stays indoors through the afternoon, and the dust storms called aandhi can turn the sky brown. In that kind of heat, even the proudest person slows down and looks for shade. Nobody walks tall at two in the afternoon in Jeth. And this is the month Guru Arjan chooses to talk about the One before whom every head goes down.
screen: `MAY INTO JUNE: THE ROADS SHIMMER.` → `EVERYONE LOOKS FOR SHADE.` → `EVERY HEAD GOES DOWN.`

segments.voice: The Jeth stanza is on ang 134. It opens, in paraphrase: in Jeth, the longing is to be joined with the Lord, before whom everyone bows. Not some. Everyone. Kings and laborers, the clever and the simple, the powerful and the poor: all of them, sooner or later, are lowered. The heat of Jeth makes that easy to picture. Then the stanza gives an image of safety. One who holds on to the hem of the beloved Friend's robe can't be bound by anyone. It's an old picture, a child or a petitioner holding the edge of someone's garment, clinging and protected. And then a picture of riches. The Name of the One, it says, is like rubies and pearls, and no thief can break in to steal them. Think about that in a hot month in an old village. Valuables could be stolen. Houses could be broken into. Here is wealth that no one can carry off. The stanza goes on to say that the One does whatever pleases the One, and creatures act accordingly; that those the One makes His own are called blessed. And it ends: in Jeth, the joyful Lord is met by the one whose forehead carries that good fortune. Put the pieces together. Bowing, holding on, a treasure that can't be stolen. Jeth's lesson isn't about pushing through the heat on your own strength. It's about lowering yourself and holding on. In a month when everything outside presses down on you, the stanza turns the pressure into a bow.
screen: `BEFORE WHOM EVERYONE BOWS.` · `HOLDING THE HEM OF THE FRIEND.` · `JEWELS NO THIEF CAN STEAL.` · `THE PRESSURE BECOMES A BOW.` · then, large: `JETH: BOW.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: bow once in the heat. Wherever you are, notice one pressure on you right now: tiredness, a deadline, actual heat, a weight in the chest. Don't push against it. Sit up, breathe in, and as you breathe out, lower your head slowly, as if bowing to something greater than the pressure. Stay low for a breath or two. Picture holding the edge of a friend's robe. Then rise slowly. If you pray, you can say Waheguru as you bow. The bell holds the time.
Jeth. The month of hard heat, when Guru Arjan longs to be joined with the One before whom everyone bows, whose Name is a treasure no thief can steal.
Your line: jeth: bow. Today, at the hottest or hardest moment of your afternoon, lower your head for one breath instead of pushing through. Day five hundred sixty-eight.

569.title: The month of Asarh
569.hook: in Asarh the heat burns those who don't have the Lord near (Barah Maha, ang 134)
569.howItsDone: On the sangrand of Asarh, gurdwaras that keep the day read the Asarh stanza of Guru Arjan's Barah Maha, as the summer heat waits on the rains.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Jeth, and your line: jeth: bow. Did you lower your head in the hardest moment? The heat isn't over. In Asarh it presses on, and the rains still haven't come. Day five hundred sixty-nine.

June into July. The fields are cracked. The canals run low. Everyone keeps looking at the sky, waiting for the monsoon, and every day the clouds gather and then don't break. People sleep on rooftops for a breath of air. The heat in Asarh isn't only on the skin; it wears on tempers, on patience, on sleep. Some people get short and sharp in weather like that. Maybe you're one of them. Guru Arjan looked at that burning month and saw something in it: the same heat doesn't land the same way on everyone.
screen: `CRACKED FIELDS, WAITING FOR RAIN.` → `SLEEPING ON ROOFTOPS.` → `THE SAME HEAT, NOT THE SAME FOR ALL.`

segments.voice: The Asarh stanza is on ang 134. In paraphrase: in Asarh, the heat scorches those whose Husband Lord isn't near them. Then he says why. They've left the One who is the life of the world, and put their hope in mortal people. Caught up in duality, in what is second, they're ruined, and death's noose is around their neck. As they sow, so they reap; what is written comes to pass. Then a picture of a whole life passing like a night: the night slips by, she regrets it, and she leaves without hope. And then the turn: Asarh is pleasant, the stanza says, for the one in whose heart the Lord's feet dwell. Same month. Same heat. For one person it's a furnace, for another it's bearable, even pleasant. The difference isn't the weather. It's what's near. There's a careful line in the middle worth slowing on: they put their hope in mortal people. Guru Arjan isn't saying don't rely on anyone. Sikh life is built on sangat, community. The problem is resting your whole hope on people who are themselves passing, who will get tired and short in the heat too. When everything you lean on is also burning, there's nowhere cool to stand. Notice also the line about sowing and reaping. In a farming month, waiting for rain, any farmer knows a harvest is the fruit of what was planted. Guru Arjan uses that knowledge plainly: a life gives back what was sown. And the stanza's cool center is still the same image: the Lord's feet dwelling in the heart. Keep the One near, and the heat changes.
screen: `THE HEAT BURNS THOSE FAR FROM THE ONE.` · `HOPE IN MORTALS, WHO ALSO BURN.` · `AS YOU SOW, SO YOU REAP.` · `THE LORD'S FEET IN THE HEART.` · then, large: `ASARH: KEEP HIM NEAR.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: cool someone down. Sit and breathe slowly, imagining cool air on the out-breath. Then think of someone in your life who's running hot right now: stressed, short-tempered, overwhelmed. Don't judge their heat. Picture bringing them something cool: a glass of water, a calm word, ten minutes of help, simply not adding to their pressure. Choose one small, concrete thing you can actually do today. If you pray, you can say Waheguru for them. The bell holds the time.
Asarh. The heat before the rains: it scorches those far from the One, and is pleasant for the one in whose heart the Lord's feet dwell.
Your line: asarh: keep him near. Today, bring your cool thing to the person you pictured, and when you feel your own temper heating, breathe out slowly once. Day five hundred sixty-nine.

570.title: The month of Sawan
570.hook: in Sawan the bride blossoms who loves His lotus feet (Barah Maha, ang 134)
570.howItsDone: On the sangrand of Sawan, many gurdwaras read the Sawan stanza of Guru Arjan's Barah Maha, while in Punjab the monsoon month is also marked by the folk festival of Teeyan.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Asarh, and your line: asarh: keep him near. Who did you cool down? After all that waiting, the clouds finally break. Day five hundred seventy.

Anyone who has lived through a North Indian summer remembers the first real rain. The smell hits before the drops do: wet dust, sharp and sweet. Then the sky opens. Kids run out into the street. Peacocks call from the fields. Within days, cracked brown ground turns green, and in Punjabi villages, swings go up in the trees, and girls and women gather to sing the songs of Teeyan. Sawan, July into August, is the month the whole land seems to exhale. And in the folk barah maha, it's the month the waiting bride feels most alive, and most alone.
screen: `THE SMELL OF THE FIRST RAIN.` → `BROWN GROUND TURNS GREEN.` → `SWINGS IN THE TREES.`

segments.voice: The Sawan stanza is on ang 134. In paraphrase: in Sawan, the bride blossoms who loves the lotus feet of the Lord. Sarsee, she blossoms, she flourishes, the way the land does when the rain comes. Her mind and body are dyed in true love; the Name alone is her support. Then a contrast. The pleasures of poison, as the stanza calls them, are false; everything that's seen of them turns to ash. And then the rain image, turned inside out. The drop of the Lord's nectar is beautiful, the stanza says, and those who meet the holy ones drink it in. The forests and the meadows are refreshed by the One, the all-powerful, the infinite. Look at what Guru Arjan does with the monsoon. In the folk songs, the rain is what makes the separated woman ache: everyone else is together under the swings. In this stanza, the rain is what happens to the soul that loves the One. She's the land. The love is the rain. And she doesn't just survive the season; she blossoms. Sawan is the first month in this Barah Maha that sounds almost like arrival. It isn't all joy; the warning about false pleasures turning to ash is still there. But the main image is green. After two months of heat, Jeth and Asarh, where the lesson was bowing and keeping the One near, Sawan shows what that kind of nearness looks like when it rains. The lotus feet, charan kamal, is an old and tender image in Indian devotion, and Gurbani uses it often: the Beloved's feet, soft as a lotus, are where the devotee comes to rest.
screen: `SARSEE: SHE BLOSSOMS.` · `FALSE PLEASURES TURN TO ASH.` · `A DROP OF THE LORD'S NECTAR.` · `THE SOUL IS THE LAND; LOVE IS THE RAIN.` · then, large: `SAWAN: BLOSSOM.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: watch rain or water. If it's raining where you are, watch it at a window. If not, run a tap slowly, or pour a glass of water and watch it fill, or simply picture rain on dry ground. Notice the first drops darkening the dust. Breathe slowly and let the picture soften something in you that's been dry. Let it be watered without needing to understand it. If you pray, you can say Waheguru with each slow breath. The bell holds the time.
Sawan. The monsoon month: the bride who loves the Lord's lotus feet blossoms, like land under the rain, and drinks the drop of nectar.
Your line: sawan: blossom. Today, water one thing: a plant, a friendship, a neglected part of your own day. Day five hundred seventy.

571.title: The month of Bhadon
571.hook: in Bhadon she is lost in doubt, attached to what is second (Barah Maha, ang 134)
571.howItsDone: On the sangrand of Bhadon, gurdwaras that keep the day read the Bhadon stanza of Guru Arjan's Barah Maha, with its warning against bharam and its promise of the One's sanctuary.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Sawan, and your line: sawan: blossom. What did you water? The rains go on, but the air turns heavy. Bhadon is the month the green starts to feel close and confusing. Day five hundred seventy-one.

The rain has stopped being a relief. Clothes won't dry. Mosquitoes are everywhere. This is Bhadon, roughly August into September, the sticky end of the monsoon. The air is so thick it's hard to think, and the paths that were clear in spring are overgrown and muddy. It's easy to lose your way in a field in Bhadon. And Guru Arjan says the soul can lose its way too, in a fog that feels a lot like that weather. He has a word for that fog.
screen: `AUGUST INTO SEPTEMBER: STICKY AIR.` → `PATHS OVERGROWN AND MUDDY.` → `A WORD FOR THE FOG.`

segments.voice: The word is bharam. The Bhadon stanza on ang 134 opens, in paraphrase: in Bhadon, she has lost her way in bharam, attached to the second. Bharam is often translated doubt, but that can mislead. In Gurbani it's not the honest question a curious person asks. It's closer to delusion, wandering, a mind going round in circles in the fog. And doojaa, the second, is Gurbani's word for duality: loving something else in place of the One. Then the stanza gets hard. She may adorn herself in a hundred thousand ways, but it accomplishes nothing. On the day the body perishes, people will speak of it as a ghost. Death's messengers seize and lead her away, and tell no one their secret. Those she was attached to every day leave her standing in a moment. She wrings her hands; her body writhes; the black hair has turned white. As she sows, so she reaps: karma is the field. It's a vivid, uncomfortable picture, and it's meant to be. Bhadon's heavy air is the stanza's picture of a life spent in the fog, decorated on the outside, lost on the inside, waking up only when it's too late to plant anything new. But the stanza doesn't end there. Nanak seeks the One's sanctuary, it says, and the One gives the boat of His feet. Those protected by the Guru aren't thrown into hell in Bhadon. So the fog has an exit. Not by thinking harder, not by more adornment. By taking refuge. The boat is the same image as the Guru's boat in the Asa di Var: what carries you across when you can't find the path on foot.
screen: `BHARAM: LOST IN THE FOG.` · `DOOJAA: LOVING THE SECOND.` · `A HUNDRED ADORNMENTS, NO USE.` · `THE BOAT OF THE ONE'S FEET.` · then, large: `BHADON: DOUBT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: name one doubt. Not an honest question; those are welcome. A fog. Sit and breathe slowly. Find one place where your mind keeps circling without getting anywhere: a worry you replay, a choice you keep avoiding, a confusion about what really matters. Name it plainly in one sentence. Naming it can thin the fog a little. Then picture stepping into a boat that carries you across, without having to figure it all out first. If you pray, you can say Waheguru. The bell holds the time.
Bhadon. The heavy end of the rains, when the soul is lost in bharam, attached to the second, until it takes refuge in the boat of the One's feet.
Your line: bhadon: doubt. Today, when you notice your mind circling, say the line and name the fog out loud. Then take one small step out of it. Day five hundred seventy-one.

572.title: The month of Assu
572.hook: in Assu love wells up: how can I meet the Lord (Barah Maha, ang 135)
572.howItsDone: On the Sangrand that begins Assu, gurdwaras that keep the day read Guru Arjan's Assu stanza from the Barah Maha in Raag Majh, often with a short talk on its meaning for the month ahead.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Bhadon, and your line: bhadon: doubt. Did you name one doubt, even quietly, to yourself? Bhadon left the bride lost and unsure. Today the rains end, and something in her starts to move. Day five hundred seventy-two.

By Assu, roughly mid-September to mid-October in Punjab, the monsoon has usually blown itself out. The mud dries, the nights cool, and the sky goes a hard, clear blue, the kind where you can suddenly see the far hills that were hidden all summer. Doubt is a lot like the rainy season. While it lasts, you can't see past the next puddle. Then one morning the air clears, and what's left isn't certainty. It's wanting. You can see where you'd like to go, and you have no idea how to get there. That is exactly where Guru Arjan's Assu stanza begins.
screen: `ASSU: THE RAINS END, THE SKY CLEARS.` → `DOUBT GIVES WAY TO WANTING.` → `BUT HOW DO I GET THERE?`

segments.voice: Here's the stanza's opening, in paraphrase: in Assu, love wells up. How can I go and meet the Lord? In Gurmukhi it begins asun prem umaahrraa. Prem is love. Umaahrraa is eagerness, a surge that rises on its own. Then comes the question that gives today its line: kiau milee-ai, how can I meet? Mind and body, the stanza says, are thirsty for a sight of the Beloved. And the bride does something very human. She calls out, O mother, will someone come and bring me to Him? Notice that the Barah Maha doesn't scold her for asking. In the Sikh reading, the question is the first step. Bhadon was confusion, attached to second things. Assu is the same person, now pointed in one direction, even if she doesn't know the road. The stanza then answers, gently. The saints, it says, are the helpers of love, and she falls at their feet. In Sikh life that points to the sangat, the company of people who are also on the way, and to the Guru's word they sing together. Without the Lord, the stanza asks, how can there be peace? There is no other place to go. And it closes on grace: in Assu, those live in peace on whom the Lord shows mercy. So the answer to how isn't a technique. It's company, and longing, and a door opened from the other side. The not-knowing is allowed.
screen: `PREM UMAAHRRAA: LOVE WELLS UP.` · `KIAU MILEE-AI: HOW CAN I MEET?` · `THE SAINTS ARE LOVE'S HELPERS.` · `PEACE COMES BY MERCY.` · then, large: `ASSU: HOW TO MEET.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: one line of longing. Sit comfortably and let your breathing slow. Ask yourself, honestly, what you long for underneath the to-do list. Peace, closeness, forgiveness, a sense of being found. Let it be simple. If you pray, you can carry the stanza's own question on the breath: kiau milee-ai, how can I meet You? If you don't pray, just let the longing be there, without fixing it or explaining it. Breathe in the wanting. Breathe out the hurry. The bell holds the time.
Assu. In Guru Arjan's Barah Maha, Assu is when love wells up and asks how to meet, and the stanza answers: through the holy company, and by mercy.
Your line: assu: how to meet. Today, when you notice yourself wanting something deeper, don't push it away. Ask the question instead, and see who turns up to help. Day five hundred seventy-two.

573.title: The month of Katak
573.hook: in Katak we reap what we did; blame no one else (Barah Maha, ang 135)
573.howItsDone: On the Sangrand of Katak, gurdwaras that keep the day read the Katak stanza of Guru Arjan's Barah Maha; it is heard as a call to take responsibility for their deeds while trusting in the Guru's grace.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Assu, and your line: assu: how to meet. Did a longing come up, and did you let it ask its question? Today the Barah Maha turns from longing to honesty. Day five hundred seventy-three.

A dent appears on the family car. Nobody did it. The kids didn't, the spouse didn't, the neighbor's teenager is the obvious suspect, and the shopping cart in the parking lot is a close second. Everyone has a story, and in every story the dent happened to them. It's an old habit: when something goes wrong, the first thing the mind builds is an alibi. Katak, in the Punjabi calendar, falls roughly from mid-October to mid-November, the season when the crops that were sown come in. And Guru Arjan's Katak stanza opens with a line that takes the alibi apart.
screen: `A DENT THAT NOBODY MADE.` → `THE MIND BUILDS AN ALIBI.` → `KATAK: HARVEST SEASON.`

segments.voice: The stanza begins katak karam kamaavane, dos na kaahoo jog. In paraphrase: in Katak, we earn what our deeds earn; no one else is to be blamed. Karam here is deeds, what you've actually done. Kamaavane is the everyday Punjabi word for earning, the way you earn wages. And dos is fault, blame. So the line is almost a farmer's line: what you planted is what's in the field. No point shouting at the neighbor's crop. Then the stanza says where the trouble really starts. Forgetting the Lord, every illness takes hold. Turning your face away, you are separated, life after life. And the pleasures of the world, it says, turn bitter in an instant. So the deepest deed in the stanza isn't stealing or lying. It's forgetting. Now, this is not a stanza of doom. Sikh teaching holds deeds and grace together. You reap what you sow, and the Guru's mercy can still reach the field. And the stanza ends with the way out: in Katak, in the company of the holy, all worries fall away. Notice what owning a fault does. While you're busy blaming, you're stuck, because only the other person can fix it. The moment you say, that one was mine, you can do something. You can apologize, repair, plant differently. Blaming no one isn't the same as blaming yourself harshly. It's simply standing in your own field, honestly, and starting from there. Diwali, and with it the Sikh Bandi Chhor Divas, usually falls in this season of harvest, a festival of lamps for a month about seeing clearly.
screen: `KARAM KAMAAVANE: WE EARN OUR DEEDS.` · `THE ROOT DEED IS FORGETTING.` · `HOLY COMPANY: WORRIES FALL AWAY.` · `OWNING IT LETS YOU ACT.` · then, large: `KATAK: BLAME NO ONE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: own one mistake. Sit comfortably and let the breath settle. Think back over the last week and find one small thing that went wrong where you'd been telling a story about someone else. A missed message, a sharp reply, a forgotten promise. Without punishing yourself, just say inwardly: that part was mine. Notice how it feels to set the alibi down. Then think of one small repair, a message, a word, a different choice next time. If you pray, you can rest in Waheguru between breaths. The bell holds the time.
Katak. In the Barah Maha, Katak is the honest month: we earn what our deeds earn, no one else is to blame, and the holy company lifts the worry.
Your line: katak: blame no one. Today, when something goes wrong, catch the first alibi as it forms, and ask what part of this is mine. Then fix that part. Day five hundred seventy-three.

574.title: The month of Maghar
574.hook: in Maghar lovely are those who sit with the Beloved (Barah Maha, ang 135)
574.howItsDone: In the gurdwara, Sikhs sit together on the floor of the diwan hall, at one level, to hear kirtan; on the Sangrand of Maghar gurdwaras that keep the day read Guru Arjan's Maghar stanza from the Barah Maha.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Katak, and your line: katak: blame no one. Did you catch an alibi as it formed? This week walked through six months: Jeth's bowing, Asarh's heat, Sawan's blossom, Bhadon's doubt, Assu's question, Katak's honesty. Today, the week ends sitting down together. Day five hundred seventy-four.

Some good hours happen with nothing going on. A kitchen late at night, two people with tea, the dishes not done. A hospital waiting room where a friend just sits beside you and doesn't try to say anything wise. A grandparent on a bench, holding a small hand, watching pigeons. Nobody would put these moments on a highlight reel. But they can be the ones that stay. Maghar, roughly mid-November to mid-December, is when the Punjabi cold starts to come in, and people pull their chairs closer. Guru Arjan's Maghar stanza is about exactly that: sitting with.
screen: `TEA AT A LATE KITCHEN TABLE.` → `A FRIEND IN THE WAITING ROOM.` → `MAGHAR: SITTING WITH.`

segments.voice: The stanza opens, in paraphrase: in Maghar, lovely are those who sit with the Beloved, the Lord. Sohandee-aa, lovely, shining. And baithrree-aah, those who sit. That's all they're doing. They aren't climbing, earning or proving. They're seated beside the One they love, and the stanza says their beauty can't even be counted. Then it adds the other side. Those who don't sit in the company of the holy, it says, stay alone. Their pain doesn't leave them, and they fall into death's grip. There's a whole Sikh practice inside that one picture. Think of the diwan hall of a gurdwara. People take off their shoes, cover their heads, bow, and then sit on the floor, together, at the same level. Nobody has a better chair. They sit while the hymns are sung, sometimes for a long time, sometimes saying nothing at all. That's sangat, the holy company, and in the Barah Maha it's where the bride finds the Beloved's presence. Look back at the week and you can see the road. In Jeth she bowed. In Asarh she learned to keep Him near in the heat. In Sawan she blossomed, in Bhadon she doubted, in Assu she longed and asked how. In Katak she stopped blaming. And now, in Maghar, she simply sits. The stanza ends: in Maghar, those who worship the Lord are not born again into the round of coming and going. The long journey of the months arrives somewhere very still. Lovely are the ones who sit.
screen: `SOHANDEE-AA: LOVELY ARE THOSE WHO SIT.` · `APART FROM THE HOLY, WE STAY ALONE.` · `SANGAT: SEATED ON ONE FLOOR.` · `THE WEEK'S ROAD ARRIVES IN STILLNESS.` · then, large: `MAGHAR: SIT TOGETHER.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: sit with someone you love. If someone you love is near, sit beside them now, no phone, no agenda, just two people in the same room. If no one is near, bring one person to mind and sit as if they were next to you. Picture their face, their hands, the way they settle into a chair. Don't plan a conversation. Just be with. If you pray, you can rest in Waheguru between breaths, the One the stanza calls the Beloved. The bell holds the time.
Maghar. In the Barah Maha, Maghar is the month of sitting: lovely are those who sit with the Beloved, and the holy company is where we sit.
Your line: maghar: sit together. Today, give one person ten minutes of sitting with them and nothing else. Tea counts. A bench counts. Day five hundred seventy-four.
